results.title: Create a Safety & Security Framework
results.requirement: Define a state-of-the-art Safety and Security Framework that conceptually describes how systemic risks are assessed, accepted, and mitigated across the model lifecycle.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define, at a conceptual and descriptive level, the key elements required for systemic risk management under the Safety and Security Chapter (including trigger points, risk acceptance logic, mitigation expectations, responsibility allocation, external input, and update processes)?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly describes its purpose as managing systemic risks associated with general-purpose AI models.
The framework outlines how systemic risks are identified, assessed, and mitigated at a high level.
The framework describes trigger points at which additional evaluations or assessments would occur during the model lifecycle.
The framework defines how systemic risk acceptability is determined, including the use of risk tiers or acceptance criteria.
The framework describes, at a high level, expected categories or types of safety and security mitigations associated with different risk levels.
The framework explains how responsibility for systemic risk assessment and mitigation is allocated within the organization.
The framework describes whether and how input from external actors may influence risk-related decisions.
The framework describes how and under what conditions the framework itself would be reviewed or updated.
results.reasoning: Evidence shows high-level lifecycle risk management (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE), accountability structures, and update/versioning processes. Missing indicators include explicit purpose for managing systemic risks, lifecycle trigger points for additional assessments, defined risk-acceptance logic with risk tiers, mapping of mitigations to risk levels, and an explicit mechanism for external input influencing risk decisions; alignment overreach notes these gaps as not clearly defined, so thematic alignment cannot substitute for these operational requirements.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: Yes — at a high level the AI Risk Management Framework (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) describes lifecycle-wide risk identification, assessment, mitigation, accountability, external input, and update processes, though it does not explicitly define concrete trigger points within the lifecycle or a prescriptive, granular risk-acceptance logic specific to systemic risks.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The framework covers high-level lifecycle risk management and governance but lacks explicit trigger points, granular risk-acceptance logic (risk tiers), explicit risk-level mitigations, and a defined mechanism for external input to risk decisions.
missing_elements: Explicit articulation of the framework’s purpose to manage systemic risks associated with general-purpose AI models.
Explicit lifecycle trigger points that would prompt additional evaluations or assessments during the model lifecycle.
Explicit systemic risk acceptance logic with defined risk tiers or acceptance criteria.
Explicit mapping of expected mitigations to different risk levels (types of mitigations per risk tier).
Explicit mechanism showing how external input from external actors influences risk-related decisions.
weaker_areas: Mitigations are described at a high level but are not explicitly tied to specific risk severity levels, reducing prescriptiveness for different systemic risk levels.
scope_divergences: Divergence: No explicit mechanism for external input into risk decisions (EU requirement emphasizes input from external actors influencing risk-related decisions).
Divergence: Trigger points for reassessment are not explicitly defined (EU expectation includes concrete lifecycle trigger points for additional evaluations).
Divergence: No explicit risk-tiered acceptance criteria mapping to systemic risk (EU expectation includes defined risk acceptance logic across risk levels).
alignment_overreach: Claim that the framework provides explicit trigger points and prescriptive, granular risk-acceptance logic for systemic risks is not supported by the retrieved text.
Claim that external input clearly influences risk decisions is not supported; the text shows broad audience usage but lacks a defined external-input decision mechanism.
Claim that the framework explicitly defines risk-level mitigations linked to different risk levels is not clearly demonstrated in the provided material.

may consider leveraging available standards and guidance that provide broad guidance to
organizations to reduce security and privacy risks, such as, but not limited to, the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, the NIST Privacy Framework, the NIST Risk Management Framework, and the Secure Software Development Framework. These frameworks have some
features in common with the AI RMF. Like most risk management approaches, they are
outcome-based rather than prescriptive and are often structured around a Core set of functions, categories, and subcategories. While there are significant differences between these
frameworks based on the domain addressed – and because AI risk management calls for
addressing many other types of risks – frameworks like those mentioned above may inform
security and privacy considerations in the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions of the
AI RMF.
At the same time, guidance available before publication of this AI RMF does not comprehensively address many AI system risks. For example, existing frameworks and guidance
are unable to:
• adequately manage the problem of harmful bias in AI systems;
• confront the challenging risks related to generative AI;
• comprehensively address security concerns related to evasion, model extraction, membership inference, availability, or other machine learning attacks;
• account for the complex attack surface of AI systems or other security abuses enabled
by AI systems; and

selected_evidence.text:
Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

Organizations need to establish and maintain the appropriate accountability mechanisms,
roles and responsibilities, culture, and incentive structures for risk management to be effective. Use of the AI RMF alone will not lead to these changes or provide the appropriate
incentives. Effective risk management is realized through organizational commitment at
senior levels and may require cultural change within an organization or industry. In addition, small to medium-sized organizations managing AI risks or implementing the AI RMF
may face different challenges than large organizations, depending on their capabilities and
resources.

across the AI lifecycle and dimensions.

results.title: Implement the Safety & Security Framework
results.requirement: Describe how the Safety and Security Framework is intended to be applied across the entire model lifecycle, including continuous systemic risk assessment activities, trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, incident inputs, and escalation to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how its systemic risk assessment and mitigation processes are intended to be applied across the model lifecycle, including continuous assessment activities, trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, incident consideration, and escalation to a full systemic risk assessment?
expected_evidence: The framework describes how systemic risks are continuously assessed along the entire model lifecycle.
The framework explains how lighter-touch evaluations are conducted at predefined trigger points (e.g. based on time, development stage, compute, access, or affordances).
The framework describes how post-market monitoring is conducted to inform ongoing systemic risk assessment.
The framework explains how information about serious incidents or near misses is taken into account within the risk assessment process.

The framework describes how results from trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, or incident inputs can lead to deeper analysis or escalation to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process.
The framework outlines the sequence or structure of the full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (identification, analysis, acceptability determination, mitigation, and re-assessment).
results.reasoning: Gap analysis flags alignment_overreach for all six indicators, treating them as unmet due to the text providing only high-level lifecycle governance and conceptual monitoring without an explicit end-to-end systemic risk assessment process, trigger-point mechanisms, distinct post-market monitoring, formal integration of incident inputs, escalation pathways, or a defined identification–analysis–acceptability–mitigation–re-assessment sequence.
key_aligned_concepts: Lifecycle governance framework (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE)
Continuous monitoring and incident contingency
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: No explicit end-to-end systemic risk assessment and mitigation process across the lifecycle (including a defined sequence: identification, analysis, acceptability, mitigation, re-assessment).
No defined trigger-point evaluations with thresholds or explicit lighter-touch risk assessments at predefined points.
Post-market monitoring described only in general terms; lacks a distinct, operational post-market monitoring program.
Incidents/near-misses acknowledged but not explicitly integrated as inputs into a formal risk assessment workflow.
No clear escalation mechanism to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process.
No explicit linking of trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, or incident inputs to deeper analysis or escalation.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The framework provides high-level governance across the AI lifecycle and mentions ongoing monitoring and incident contingency, but it does not explicitly describe a full, end-to-end systemic risk assessment and mitigation process with trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring as distinct from general monitoring, escalation to a complete systemic risk assessment, or the defined sequence of identification–analysis–acceptability–mitigation–re-assessment.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: Aligns at a conceptual level with lifecycle governance and ongoing risk management, but lacks explicit trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring distinct from general monitoring, escalation mechanisms, and a detailed end-to-end risk assessment sequence as required.
key_aligned_concepts: Lifecycle governance framework (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE)
Continuous monitoring and incident contingency

evidence_citations.quote: The MAP function establishes the context to frame risks related to an AI system. The AI lifecycle consists of many interdependent activities involving a diverse set of actors (See Figure 3). In practice, AI actors in charge of one part of the process often do not have full visibility or control over other parts and their associated contexts. As a result, the best intentions within one dimension of the AI lifecycle can be undermined via interactions with decisions and conditions in other, later activities.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Demonstrates lifecycle-spanning governance context and cross-actor risk framing.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: SS-1.2: Continuous systemic risk assessment across lifecycle (conceptual)

evidence_citations.quote: GOVERN 6.2: Contingency processes are in place to handle failures or incidents in third-party data or AI systems deemed to be high-risk.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Demonstrates incident handling consideration, a component of risk assessment inputs.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: SS-1.2: Incident inputs and contingency handling (conceptual)

evidence_citations.quote: MANAGE 3: AI risks and benefits from third-party resources are regularly monitored, and risk controls are applied and documented.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Supports ongoing monitoring as part of risk management during deployment.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: SS-1.2: Post-market/continuous monitoring (conceptual)

evidence_citations.quote: After completing the MANAGE function, plans for prioritizing risk and regular monitoring and improvement will be in place.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Indicates ongoing monitoring and improvement, a component of lifecycle risk management.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: SS-1.2: Post-deployment monitoring and improvement (conceptual)

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The framework lacks an explicit end-to-end systemic risk assessment and mitigation process across the lifecycle, including defined trigger-point evaluations, distinct post-market monitoring, incorporation of incident inputs, and formal escalation pathways to a full systemic risk assessment.
missing_elements: Explicit description of trigger-point evaluations (lighter-touch risk assessments) at predefined points along the model lifecycle.
Explicit description of post-market monitoring as a distinct, ongoing systemic risk activity, including methods, data inputs, responsibilities, and review cadence.
Clear mechanism for incorporating serious incidents or near misses as inputs to the systemic risk assessment with defined processes and thresholds.

Description of how results from trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, or incident inputs lead to deeper analysis and escalation to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process, including the decision criteria.
Defined sequence of the full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (identification, analysis, acceptability determination, mitigation, and re-assessment) tied to lifecycle stages.
weaker_areas: High-level lifecycle governance is present, but there is no explicit end-to-end systemic risk assessment process or linkage to trigger points and escalation.
Post-market monitoring is mentioned only in a general sense; no distinct, elaborated methodology or practices are described.
Incidents are acknowledged in contingency terms, but there is no explicit integration of incident inputs into a formal risk assessment workflow.
scope_divergences: EU requirement calls for an end-to-end, lifecycle-spanning systemic risk assessment and mitigation process with a defined sequence (identification–analysis–acceptability–mitigation–re-assessment); the text does not provide this sequence or its integration across lifecycle stages.
EU requirement requires trigger-point evaluations with clear thresholds; the text does not describe any trigger-point mechanism or criteria.

EU requirement requires post-market monitoring described as a distinct activity informing ongoing systemic risk assessment; the text provides only general monitoring language without a distinct post-market framework.
EU requirement requires escalation pathways to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process; the text lacks explicit escalation mechanisms and responsibilities.
EU requirement requires explicit integration of incident inputs (serious incidents/near misses) into the risk assessment process; the text does not articulate how such inputs feed risk assessments.
alignment_overreach: SS-1.2: Continuous systemic risk assessment across lifecycle (described as conceptual in alignment notes but not explicitly implemented in the text).
SS-1.2: Post-market/continuous monitoring described as conceptual rather than a defined, distinct post-market monitoring program.
SS-1.2: Incident inputs and contingency handling described as conceptual inputs to risk assessment without an explicit integration into a formal risk assessment workflow.
SS-1.2: Trigger-point evaluations and escalation to a full systemic risk assessment described as conceptual rather than defined procedures with thresholds and roles.
SS-1.2: Defined sequence of the full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (identification–analysis–acceptability–mitigation–re-assessment) not actually described in the retrieved text.

synthesis_result.justification: Gap analysis flags alignment_overreach for all six indicators, treating them as unmet due to the text providing only high-level lifecycle governance and conceptual monitoring without an explicit end-to-end systemic risk assessment process, trigger-point mechanisms, distinct post-market monitoring, formal integration of incident inputs, escalation pathways, or a defined identification–analysis–acceptability–mitigation–re-assessment sequence.

5.2
Map
The MAP function establishes the context to frame risks related to an AI system. The AI
lifecycle consists of many interdependent activities involving a diverse set of actors (See
Figure 3). In practice, AI actors in charge of one part of the process often do not have full
visibility or control over other parts and their associated contexts. The interdependencies
between these activities, and among the relevant AI actors, can make it difficult to reliably
anticipate impacts of AI systems. For example, early decisions in identifying purposes and
objectives of an AI system can alter its behavior and capabilities, and the dynamics of deployment setting (such as end users or impacted individuals) can shape the impacts of AI
system decisions. As a result, the best intentions within one dimension of the AI lifecycle
can be undermined via interactions with decisions and conditions in other, later activities.
Page 24
NIST AI 100-1
AI RMF 1.0
This complexity and varying levels of visibility can introduce uncertainty into risk management practices. Anticipating, assessing, and otherwise addressing potential sources of
negative risk can mitigate this uncertainty and enhance the integrity of the decision process.

Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.

5.4
Manage
The MANAGE function entails allocating risk resources to mapped and measured risks on
a regular basis and as defined by the GOVERN function. Risk treatment comprises plans to
respond to, recover from, and communicate about incidents or events.
Contextual information gleaned from expert consultation and input from relevant AI actors
– established in GOVERN and carried out in MAP – is utilized in this function to decrease
the likelihood of system failures and negative impacts. Systematic documentation practices
established in GOVERN and utilized in MAP and MEASURE bolster AI risk management
efforts and increase transparency and accountability. Processes for assessing emergent risks
are in place, along with mechanisms for continual improvement.
After completing the MANAGE function, plans for prioritizing risk and regular monitoring
and improvement will be in place. Framework users will have enhanced capacity to manage the risks of deployed AI systems and to allocate risk management resources based on
assessed and prioritized risks. It is incumbent on Framework users to continue to apply
the MANAGE function to deployed AI systems as methods, contexts, risks, and needs or
expectations from relevant AI actors evolve over time.

results.title: Framework updates
results.requirement: Describe how the Safety and Security Framework defines the conditions, processes, and scope for periodic and event-driven framework assessments and updates, including versioning, changelogs, and remediation planning, in line with Measure 1.3 of the Safety and Security Chapter.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define how and when framework assessments and updates are intended to occur, including assessment triggers, periodic review, evaluation of framework adequacy and adherence, and the handling of remediation and versioning?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that it is subject to periodic reassessment (e.g. at defined intervals) and to reassessment when specified conditions or events occur.

The framework describes conditions or triggers that would lead to a framework assessment (e.g. material changes in model development, serious incidents or near misses, materially changed systemic risks or model capabilities).
The framework explains the scope of a framework assessment, including the evaluation of framework adequacy with respect to the systemic risks of the models.
The framework explains that framework adherence is assessed, including consideration of non-adherence and its causes.
The framework describes how findings from a framework assessment may lead to updates of the framework to keep it state-of-the-art.
The framework describes that updates are intended to be versioned and accompanied by a changelog explaining the nature and rationale of changes.
The framework describes how remediation plans are intended to be defined when framework assessments identify risks of continued or future non-adherence.
results.reasoning: Found indicators for versioning with a changelog (Indicator 6) and a semi-annual review cadence (Indicator 1) plus a living-document stance supporting updates (Indicator 5). Missing explicit assessment triggers (Indicator 2), explicit periodic/event-driven assessments beyond the cadence, formal adherence evaluation (Indicator 4), remediation planning (Indicator 7), defined scope of assessments (Indicator 3), and a clear mechanism showing how assessment findings drive state-of-the-art updates (Indicator 5).
key_aligned_concepts: Versioning system with major/minor revisions and a Version Control Table
Periodic/update governance including semi-annual review of feedback
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit assessment triggers (conditions or events) that would initiate a framework assessment.
Explicit mechanism for periodic and event-driven framework assessments beyond a generic semi-annual update cadence.
Formal evaluation of framework adherence, including consideration of non-adherence and its causes.
Remediation planning process for addressing risks identified during framework assessments.
Defined scope of a framework assessment, including evaluation of adequacy with respect to systemic risks of the models.
Description of how findings from a framework assessment lead to updates to keep the framework state-of-the-art.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: Partially; the framework defines versioning, a changelog, and an intention to update frequently with a semi-annual review process, but it does not explicitly define assessment triggers, explicit periodic/event-driven assessments, formal evaluation of adherence, or remediation planning.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The text provides concrete, operational mechanisms for versioning and changelog-driven updates and a periodic review cadence, but it lacks explicit triggers for assessments, formal adherence evaluation, and remediation planning.
key_aligned_concepts: Versioning system with major/minor revisions and a Version Control Table
Periodic/update governance including semi-annual review of feedback

evidence_citations.quote: Framework will employ a two-number versioning system to track and identify major and minor changes. The first number will represent the generation of the AI RMF and its companion documents (e.g., 1.0) and will change only with major revisions. Minor revisions will be tracked using “.n” after the generation number (e.g., 1.1). All changes will be tracked using a Version Control Table which identifies the history, including version number, date of change, and description of change.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Directly documents the operational mechanism for tracking and communicating changes to the framework.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Updates are versioned and accompanied by a changelog (versioning and Version Control Table).

evidence_citations.quote: Comments on the AI RMF Playbook may be sent via email to AIframework@nist.gov at any time and will be reviewed and integrated on a semi-annual basis.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Provides an explicit cadence and channel for governance input and updates.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Periodic review process for updates (semi-annual).

evidence_citations.quote: Be a living document. The AI RMF should be readily updated as technology, understanding, and approaches to AI trustworthiness and uses of AI change and as stakeholders learn from implementing AI risk management generally and this framework in particular.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Supports ongoing governance and adaptation, aligning with the expectation of updates in response to evolving risks and knowledge.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Living document; readiness to update in response to changes.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The external framework provides versioning, a changelog, and a semi-annual review cadence but does not define explicit assessment triggers, explicit periodic/event-driven framework assessments, formal evaluation of adherence, or a remediation planning process, nor does it clearly specify the scope of framework assessments or how findings drive updates.
missing_elements: Explicit assessment triggers (conditions or events) that would initiate a framework assessment.
Explicit mechanism for periodic and event-driven framework assessments beyond a generic semi-annual update cadence.
Formal evaluation of framework adherence, including consideration of non-adherence and its causes.
Remediation planning process for addressing risks identified during framework assessments.
Defined scope of a framework assessment, including evaluation of adequacy with respect to systemic risks of the models.
Description of how findings from a framework assessment lead to updates to keep the framework state-of-the-art.
weaker_areas: Adherence evaluation is not defined; non-adherence causes and impacts are not described.
Remediation planning is not described, so there is no predefined path from findings to corrective actions.
scope_divergences: Divergence from EU requirement in that the text centers on versioning, changelogs, and input cadence (semi-annual reviews) rather than a structured governance process for triggering, conducting, and applying framework assessments and remediation.
alignment_overreach: Assessment triggers
Explicit periodic/event-driven assessments
Formal evaluation of adherence
Remediation planning

results.requirement: Acknowledge the obligation to notify the AI Office of the Safety and Security Framework and its updates, in line with Measure 1.4 of the Safety and Security Chapter.
results.assessment_question: Measure 1.4 Framework notifications: Does the framework acknowledge the obligation to notify the AI Office of the framework and its updates, including any intended notification timing?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly acknowledges an obligation to notify or inform the AI Office about the Safety and Security Framework.
The framework indicates that updates to the framework are also subject to notification.
The framework references the intended timing for such notification (e.g. after confirmation or update).
results.reasoning: None of the three Expected Evidence indicators are present: there is no formal obligation to notify the AI Office, no mechanism for notifying the AI Office about updates, and no defined notification timing. Internal versioning and a general feedback channel to NIST exist, but they do not satisfy the external AI Office notification requirement, so alignment cannot be deemed compliant.
key_aligned_concepts: Versioning and change tracking for updates
General notification/feedback channel (to the framework authors) via email
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: A formal obligation to notify the AI Office about the Safety and Security Framework.
A mechanism to notify the AI Office about updates to the Framework.
Specified timing for such notifications (e.g., after confirmation of updates).

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: No; the text does not acknowledge an obligation to notify the AI Office of the Safety and Security Framework or its updates, nor does it specify timing for such notification to the AI Office.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: There is no explicit alignment with the specific EU Measure 1.4 obligation to notify the AI Office; the document provides a general notification channel to NIST and internal versioning, but not a formal notification to the AI Office or specified timing for such notifications.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: EU Measure 1.4 requires a formal obligation to notify the AI Office about the Safety and Security Framework and its updates, including timing. The retrieved text only shows internal versioning and a general feedback channel to NIST, with no obligation or timing for notifying the AI Office.
missing_elements: A formal obligation to notify the AI Office about the Safety and Security Framework.
A mechanism to notify the AI Office about updates to the Framework.
Specified timing for such notifications (e.g., after confirmation of updates).
weaker_areas: Existing versioning and a general email feedback channel exist, but they are not binding notifications to the AI Office and are not explicitly tied to EU Measure 1.4 requirements.
Notification pathway targets NIST (and internal playbook processes) rather than the AI Office; no defined external governance notification to the AI Office.
scope_divergences: Divergence in target of notification: EU requires notification to the AI Office; the text addresses internal version control and external feedback to NIST, not to the AI Office.
Divergence in timing/triggering: EU expects a defined timing for notifying the AI Office; the text provides no such timing requirement for AI Office notifications.

Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI

4.
Effectiveness of the AI RMF
Evaluations of AI RMF effectiveness – including ways to measure bottom-line improvements in the trustworthiness of AI systems – will be part of future NIST activities, in
conjunction with the AI community.
Organizations and other users of the Framework are encouraged to periodically evaluate
whether the AI RMF has improved their ability to manage AI risks, including but not limited to their policies, processes, practices, implementation plans, indicators, measurements,
and expected outcomes. NIST intends to work collaboratively with others to develop metrics, methodologies, and goals for evaluating the AI RMF’s effectiveness, and to broadly
share results and supporting information. Framework users are expected to benefit from:
• enhanced processes for governing, mapping, measuring, and managing AI risk, and
clearly documenting outcomes;
• improved awareness of the relationships and tradeoffs among trustworthiness characteristics, socio-technical approaches, and AI risks;
• explicit processes for making go/no-go system commissioning and deployment decisions;
• established policies, processes, practices, and procedures for improving organizational accountability efforts related to AI system risks;
• enhanced organizational culture which prioritizes the identification and management
of AI system risks and potential impacts to individuals, communities, organizations,
and society;

continue to develop, and to be operationalized by organizations in varying degrees and
capacities so society can benefit from AI while also being protected from its potential
harms.
The Framework and supporting resources will be updated, expanded, and improved based
on evolving technology, the standards landscape around the world, and AI community experience and feedback. NIST will continue to align the AI RMF and related guidance with
applicable international standards, guidelines, and practices. As the AI RMF is put into
use, additional lessons will be learned to inform future updates and additional resources.

results.title: Risk identification process
results.requirement: Define a structured systemic risk identification process that is explicitly informed by the types of risks, the nature of systemic risks, and the sources of systemic risks as set out in Appendix 1, and that explicitly considers the specified systemic risks.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define a structured systemic risk identification process that is informed by the risk types (Appendix 1.1), the nature of systemic risks (Appendix 1.2), the sources of systemic risks (Appendix 1.3), and that explicitly considers the specified systemic risks (Appendix 1.4)?
expected_evidence: The framework describes a structured process for identifying systemic risks stemming from the model.

The framework indicates that potential systemic risks are initially considered with reference to the types of risks defined in Appendix 1.1 (e.g. risks to public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, and society).

The framework explains that the identification process considers the nature of systemic risks, including essential and contributing characteristics such as scale, propagation, capability-dependence, or irreversibility (Appendix 1.2).

The framework describes how potential sources of systemic risks are considered in the identification process, including model capabilities, model propensities, and model affordances or contextual factors (Appendix 1.3).

The framework explicitly indicates that the specified systemic risks listed in Appendix 1.4 are taken into account as part of the systemic risk identification process, such as risks related to chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) threats, loss of control of the model, large-scale cyber offence, and harmful manipulation.
results.reasoning: The retrieved text describes governance functions (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) and risk framing, but does not provide a structured systemic risk identification process explicitly informed by Appendix 1 risk types, nature, sources, or the Appendix 1.4 specified systemic risks. Alignment_overreach flagged in the gap analysis confirms the absence of an explicit Appendix 1–based identification workflow; therefore all indicators are unmet.
key_aligned_concepts: Framing risk and understanding risks, impacts, and harms (1.1)
Governance structure with core risk management functions (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE)
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: No explicit Appendix 1.1 risk types integrated into a systemic risk identification workflow.
No incorporation of Appendix 1.2 nature of systemic risks within the identification process.
No consideration of Appendix 1.3 sources of systemic risks within the identification process.
No explicit inclusion of Appendix 1.4 specified systemic risks (e.g., CBRN threats, loss of model control, large-scale cyber offence, harmful manipulation) in a defined identification workflow.
No mapping of Appendix 1 concepts to a defined identification step; framework relies on general governance rather than Appendix 1–based identification.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: No; the retrieved AI RMF text outlines a structured risk governance approach (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) and risk framing but does not define a structured systemic risk identification process explicitly informed by Appendix 1 types, nature, sources, and the specified systemic risks.

Incorporation of Appendix 1.3: consideration of sources of systemic risks (e.g., model capabilities, model propensities, model affordances, contextual factors) within the identification process.

results.title: Model-independent information
results.requirement: Describe how the framework defines the gathering of model-independent information relevant to systemic risk analysis, including how the breadth and depth of information gathering are determined in relation to the systemic risk.
results.assessment_question: Does the organisation systematically gather and document model-independent information relevant to identified systemic risks, using structured methods such as web searches or OSINT, literature reviews, market analyses of comparable models, training data reviews, historical incident analysis, forecasting of technological trends, expert consultations, and/or stakeholder or community engagement?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that systemic risk analysis is informed by model-independent information.
The framework explains that the breadth and depth of model-independent information gathering are adjusted based on the characteristics or severity of the systemic risk.

The framework indicates categories of methods that may be used to gather model-independent information, such as web searches or open-source intelligence, literature reviews, market analyses, reviews of historical incident data, forecasting of general trends, expert interviews or panels, and participatory or community-based research methods.

The framework clarifies the role of model-independent information in informing subsequent stages of systemic risk analysis (e.g. evaluations, modelling, or estimation), without requiring that such stages have already been performed.
results.reasoning: Indicator 1 is addressed (systemic risk analysis is informed by model-independent information via external expert input). However, indicators 2–4 are not clearly satisfied: there is no explicit scaling of breadth/depth to risk severity, no explicit catalog of methods for gathering model-independent information, and no explicit articulation that such information informs downstream risk analyses without requiring other stages to have already been performed.

Documented contextual information informs risk analysis and system design

decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit enumeration of methods for gathering model-independent information (e.g., OSINT, literature reviews, market analyses, historical incident reviews, forecasting, expert interviews/panels, participatory/community methods).

results.title: Model evaluations
results.requirement: Describe how the framework defines the design and conduct of state-of-the-art model evaluations to analyse systemic risks, in line with Appendix 3.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how model evaluations are intended to be designed and conducted to analyse systemic risks in a state-of-the-art manner, including appropriate elicitation, open-ended or adversarial testing, assessment of mitigation effectiveness, methodological rigour, and the use of qualified evaluation teams?
expected_evidence: The framework states that model evaluations are conducted.
The framework indicates that model evaluations are state-of-the-art.
The framework links model evaluations to the analysis of systemic risks.
The framework indicates that evaluations assess model capabilities, propensities, affordances, or effects.
The framework states that evaluations are designed appropriately for the model and the systemic risk.
The framework indicates that evaluations include open-ended testing to identify unexpected behaviours or emergent properties.
The framework indicates that evaluation design is informed by model-independent information.
results.reasoning: Found indicators: (1) TEVV-based evaluation processes are in place, and (3) evaluations are linked to systemic risk analysis. Missing indicators: (2) explicit state-of-the-art designation for evaluations, (4) assessment of capabilities/propensities/affordances/effects, (5) evaluations designed for the specific model and systemic risk, (6) open-ended/adversarial testing, (7) evaluation design informed by model-independent information. The alignment_overreach flagged in the gap analysis confirms these missing operational design elements; thematic language cannot fully substitute for the explicit operational requirements.
key_aligned_concepts: TEVV-based evaluation processes
Measurement informing risk management and monitoring
Identification and tracking of emergent risks
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Alignment_overreach: explicit state-of-the-art elicitation design, open-ended/adversarial testing, mitigation-effectiveness assessment, and qualified evaluation teams are not evidenced; insufficient alignment to Appendix 3 guidance.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: It partially addresses the assessment question: it describes TEVV-based measurement and risk-monitoring processes linked to AI risk management, but does not explicitly define state-of-the-art design for elicitation, open-ended/adversarial testing, mitigation effectiveness, or qualified evaluation teams.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The text describes measurement- and TEVV-driven evaluation design that ties into risk management and emergent risks, but it does not explicitly specify state-of-the-art elicitation methods, open-ended/adversarial testing, mitigation effectiveness assessment, or qualified evaluation teams.
key_aligned_concepts: TEVV-based evaluation processes
Measurement informing risk management and monitoring
Emphasis on emergent risks and open, autonomous evaluation evolution

evidence_citations.quote: After completing the MEASURE function, objective, repeatable, or scalable test, evaluation, verification, and validation (TEVV) processes including metrics, methods, and methodologies are in place, followed, and documented. Metrics and measurement methodologies should adhere to scientific, legal, and ethical norms and be carried out in an open and transparent process. New types of measurement, qualitative and quantitative, may need to be developed. The degree to which each measurement type provides unique and meaningful information to the assessment of AI risks should be considered. Framework users will enhance their capacity to comprehensively evaluate system trustworthiness, identify and track existing and emergent risks, and verify efficacy of the metrics. Measurement outcomes will be utilized in the MANAGE function to assist risk monitoring and response efforts. It is incumbent on Framework users to continue applying the MEASURE function to AI systems as knowledge, methodologies, risks, and impacts evolve over time.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The external framework discusses TEVV-based measurement and risk management with attention to emergent risks, but it does not provide explicit, state-of-the-art design for model evaluations targeting systemic risks as required by Appendix 3. Specifically, it lacks explicit elicitation methods, open-ended/adversarial testing, mitigation-effectiveness assessment, and provisions for qualified evaluation teams.
missing_elements: Explicit state-of-the-art design for elicitation methods within evaluations (e.g., structured elicitation, scenario-based elicitation).
Open-ended or adversarial testing to uncover unexpected behaviours or emergent properties.
Assessment of mitigation effectiveness within the evaluation framework.
Defined requirements for qualified evaluation teams (expertise, independence, credentials) and oversight.
Direct alignment to Appendix 3 guidance on the design and conduct of systemic-risk-focused evaluations.
Evaluation design that is explicitly tailored to the model and the systemic risk being analyzed, including use of model-independent information to inform design.
Explicit linkage showing how evaluation outcomes inform systemic risk management decisions.
weaker_areas: TEVV-based evaluation language is present but not explicitly characterized as state-of-the-art for systemic risk evaluations.
Limited detail on the use of model-independent information to inform evaluation design.
Unclear, documented mapping from evaluation results to actions in systemic risk management.
scope_divergences: Divergence: The framework focuses on TEVV, measurement, and risk management rather than providing Appendix 3–aligned, state-of-the-art design criteria for systemic-risk–focused model evaluations.
alignment_overreach: Claims of explicit state-of-the-art elicitation design.
Claims of open-ended/adversarial testing mechanisms.
Claims of explicit mitigation-effectiveness assessment within evaluations.
Claims of mandatory qualified evaluation teams.

The alignment_overreach flagged in the gap analysis confirms these missing operational design elements; thematic language cannot fully substitute for the explicit operational requirements.

Measurement informing risk management and monitoring
Identification and tracking of emergent risks

NIST AI 100-1
AI RMF 1.0
4.
Effectiveness of the AI RMF
Evaluations of AI RMF effectiveness – including ways to measure bottom-line improvements in the trustworthiness of AI systems – will be part of future NIST activities, in
conjunction with the AI community.
Organizations and other users of the Framework are encouraged to periodically evaluate
whether the AI RMF has improved their ability to manage AI risks, including but not limited to their policies, processes, practices, implementation plans, indicators, measurements,
and expected outcomes. NIST intends to work collaboratively with others to develop metrics, methodologies, and goals for evaluating the AI RMF’s effectiveness, and to broadly
share results and supporting information. Framework users are expected to benefit from:
• enhanced processes for governing, mapping, measuring, and managing AI risk, and
clearly documenting outcomes;
• improved awareness of the relationships and tradeoffs among trustworthiness characteristics, socio-technical approaches, and AI risks;
• explicit processes for making go/no-go system commissioning and deployment decisions;
• established policies, processes, practices, and procedures for improving organizational accountability efforts related to AI system risks;
• enhanced organizational culture which prioritizes the identification and management
of AI system risks and potential impacts to individuals, communities, organizations,
and society;

practices, methodologies, and tools for managing AI risks – as well as illustrate the
need for additional, improved resources.
9. Be law- and regulation-agnostic.
The Framework should support organizations’
abilities to operate under applicable domestic and international legal or regulatory
regimes.
10. Be a living document. The AI RMF should be readily updated as technology, understanding, and approaches to AI trustworthiness and uses of AI change and as stakeholders learn from implementing AI risk management generally and this framework
in particular.

NIST AI 100-1
AI RMF 1.0
Part 1: Foundational Information
1.
Framing Risk
AI risk management offers a path to minimize potential negative impacts of AI systems,
such as threats to civil liberties and rights, while also providing opportunities to maximize
positive impacts. Addressing, documenting, and managing AI risks and potential negative
impacts effectively can lead to more trustworthy AI systems.
1.1
Understanding and Addressing Risks, Impacts, and Harms
In the context of the AI RMF, risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability
of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event.
The impacts, or consequences, of AI systems can be positive, negative, or both and can
result in opportunities or threats (Adapted from: ISO 31000:2018). When considering the
negative impact of a potential event, risk is a function of 1) the negative impact, or magnitude of harm, that would arise if the circumstance or event occurs and 2) the likelihood of
occurrence (Adapted from: OMB Circular A-130:2016). Negative impact or harm can be
experienced by individuals, groups, communities, organizations, society, the environment,
and the planet.
“Risk management refers to coordinated activities to direct and control an organization with regard to risk” (Source: ISO 31000:2018).

results.title: Risk estimation
results.requirement: Describe how the framework defines the estimation of the probability and severity of harm for systemic risks, using at least state-of-the-art risk estimation methods and taking into account relevant information inputs.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how the probability and severity of harm for systemic risks are intended to be estimated using state-of-the-art methods, taking into account relevant information from systemic risk identification, analysis, and serious incident reporting, and how such estimates are expressed?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that probability and severity of harm are estimated as part of systemic risk analysis.
The framework indicates that at least state-of-the-art risk estimation methods are used, appropriate to the systemic risk being assessed.

The framework explains that risk estimation takes into account relevant information inputs, such as outputs from systemic risk identification and analysis and information about serious incidents or near misses.

The framework describes how estimates of systemic risk are expressed, for example as risk scores, risk matrices, probability distributions, or other qualitative, semi-quantitative, or quantitative formats.
The framework explains the purpose of risk estimation in supporting systemic risk acceptance determination, without requiring specific numerical or qualitative results.
results.reasoning: Gap analysis flags alignment_overreach and the Expected Evidence indicators for explicit systemic-risk estimation methods, inputs, expression formats, and acceptance purpose as unmet. The retrieved text provides high-level risk definitions and governance concepts but does not present explicit systemic-risk–specific estimation methods, inputs from systemic risk identification or incident reporting, formats for expressing systemic risk estimates, or a stated purpose to support systemic risk acceptance decisions. organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,

system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.

results.requirement: Describe how the framework defines post-market monitoring to gather information relevant to systemic risk assessment and updating, and how independent external evaluators are intended to be enabled under appropriate safeguards, where applicable.
results.assessment_question: What post-market monitoring methods are required for assessing and mitigating systemic risk, and under what conditions and safeguards must independent external evaluators be granted access to model versions, chains-of-thought, and safety-reduced model variants, including protections against legal retaliation and responsible vulnerability disclosure timelines?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that post-market monitoring is conducted to gather information about the model’s capabilities, propensities, affordances, and/or effects.

The framework describes whether and under what conditions independent external evaluators are intended to be provided with access to the model for post-market monitoring purposes.

1.2.3
Risk Prioritization
Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because
not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may

results.requirement: Describe how the framework defines decisions to proceed with, restrict, or not proceed with the development, making available on the market, or use of the model based on systemic risk acceptance determination.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how decisions to proceed or not proceed with the development, market availability, or use of the model are made based on systemic risk acceptance determination, and how responses are defined when risks are not acceptable or are likely to become unacceptable?
expected_evidence: The framework states that proceeding with development, making available on the market, or use of the model is conditional on systemic risks being determined acceptable.
The framework states that if systemic risks are not acceptable or are reasonably foreseeable to soon become unacceptable, appropriate measures must be taken before proceeding.
The framework describes possible actions when risks are not acceptable, such as not making the model available on the market, restricting availability, withdrawing, or recalling the model.
The framework states that safety and/or security mitigations are to be implemented when systemic risks are not acceptable.

The framework states that another round of systemic risk identification, systemic risk analysis, and systemic risk acceptance determination is to be conducted when risks are not acceptable or are reasonably foreseeable to soon become unacceptable.

NIST AI 100-1
AI RMF 1.0
Part 1: Foundational Information
1.
Framing Risk
AI risk management offers a path to minimize potential negative impacts of AI systems,
such as threats to civil liberties and rights, while also providing opportunities to maximize
positive impacts. Addressing, documenting, and managing AI risks and potential negative
impacts effectively can lead to more trustworthy AI systems.
1.1
Understanding and Addressing Risks, Impacts, and Harms
In the context of the AI RMF, risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability
of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event.
The impacts, or consequences, of AI systems can be positive, negative, or both and can
result in opportunities or threats (Adapted from: ISO 31000:2018). When considering the
negative impact of a potential event, risk is a function of 1) the negative impact, or magnitude of harm, that would arise if the circumstance or event occurs and 2) the likelihood of
occurrence (Adapted from: OMB Circular A-130:2016). Negative impact or harm can be
experienced by individuals, groups, communities, organizations, society, the environment,
and the planet.
“Risk management refers to coordinated activities to direct and control an organization with regard to risk” (Source: ISO 31000:2018).

Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

results.title: Safety mitigations
results.requirement: The framework defines and requires the implementation of safety mitigations along the entire model lifecycle that are appropriate to identified systemic risks, sufficiently robust under adversarial pressure, and taking into account the model’s release and distribution strategy, with the objective of ensuring that systemic risks are acceptable
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define and require the implementation of safety mitigations along the entire model lifecycle that are appropriate to identified systemic risks, sufficiently robust under adversarial pressure, and taking into account the model’s release and distribution strategy, with the objective of ensuring that systemic risks are acceptable?
expected_evidence: The framework describes categories or types of safety mitigations intended to address systemic risks.
The framework explains that safety mitigations are designed to be robust under adversarial pressure, such as attempts to bypass or subvert them.
The framework indicates that safety mitigations take into account the model's release and distribution strategy.
The framework provides examples of safety mitigation approaches, such as e.g. input or output filtering, behaviour modification, staged access, or other emerging safety techniques.
The framework indicates that safety mitigations are considered and adapted across the model lifecycle.
results.reasoning: Indicator 5 (lifecycle adaptation) is supported by evidence of lifecycle governance and context-based tailoring; indicators 1–4 (explicit mitigation categories, binding lifecycle-spanning requirements, explicit adversarial robustness, and concrete mitigation examples) are not satisfactorily evidenced. Alignment_overreach flags further that the framework does not substantiate a comprehensive, lifecycle-spanning set of mitigations tied to release/distribution; therefore, operational/normative requirements are not fully met and thematic alignment cannot fully compensate.

Real-time monitoring, intervention capabilities, and adversarial/security considerations
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Alignment overreach: framework claims to define a comprehensive lifecycle-spanning set of safety mitigations that are not supported by the text.
Missing explicit categories or types of safety mitigations intended to address systemic risks (e.g., input/output filtering, behavior modification, staged access, containment).
No binding requirement to implement and maintain safety mitigations across the entire model lifecycle, including alignment with release/distribution strategy.
No explicit requirement that safety mitigations be sufficiently robust under adversarial pressure (resistance to bypass/subversion).
No concrete mitigation examples beyond high-level governance concepts, nor a mechanism for review/update across lifecycle stages.

Robustness or generalizability is defined as the “ability of a system to maintain its level
of performance under a variety of circumstances” (Source: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Robustness is a goal for appropriate system functionality in a broad set of conditions and
circumstances, including uses of AI systems not initially anticipated. Robustness requires
not only that the system perform exactly as it does under expected uses, but also that it
should perform in ways that minimize potential harms to people if it is operating in an
unexpected setting.
Validity and reliability for deployed AI systems are often assessed by ongoing testing or
monitoring that confirms a system is performing as intended. Measurement of validity,
accuracy, robustness, and reliability contribute to trustworthiness and should take into consideration that certain types of failures can cause greater harm. AI risk management efforts
should prioritize the minimization of potential negative impacts, and may need to include
human intervention in cases where the AI system cannot detect or correct errors.

AI systems should “not under defined conditions, lead to a state in which human life,
health, property, or the environment is endangered” (Source: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Safe
operation of AI systems is improved through:
• responsible design, development, and deployment practices;
• clear information to deployers on responsible use of the system;

safety in fields such as transportation and healthcare, and align with existing sector- or
application-specific guidelines or standards.
3.3
Secure and Resilient
AI systems, as well as the ecosystems in which they are deployed, may be said to be resilient if they can withstand unexpected adverse events or unexpected changes in their environment or use – or if they can maintain their functions and structure in the face of internal
and external change and degrade safely and gracefully when this is necessary (Adapted
from: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Common security concerns relate to adversarial examples,
data poisoning, and the exfiltration of models, training data, or other intellectual property
through AI system endpoints. AI systems that can maintain confidentiality, integrity, and
availability through protection mechanisms that prevent unauthorized access and use may
be said to be secure. Guidelines in the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and Risk Management Framework are among those which are applicable here.
Security and resilience are related but distinct characteristics. While resilience is the ability to return to normal function after an unexpected adverse event, security includes resilience but also encompasses protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover
from attacks. Resilience relates to robustness and goes beyond the provenance of the data
to encompass unexpected or adversarial use (or abuse or misuse) of the model or data.

mitigation, or removal of the system from design, development, production, or use, as well
as a range of compensating, detective, deterrent, directive, and recovery controls.
After completing the MEASURE function, objective, repeatable, or scalable test, evaluation,
verification, and validation (TEVV) processes including metrics, methods, and methodologies are in place, followed, and documented. Metrics and measurement methodologies
should adhere to scientific, legal, and ethical norms and be carried out in an open and transparent process. New types of measurement, qualitative and quantitative, may need to be
developed. The degree to which each measurement type provides unique and meaningful
information to the assessment of AI risks should be considered. Framework users will enhance their capacity to comprehensively evaluate system trustworthiness, identify and track
existing and emergent risks, and verify efficacy of the metrics. Measurement outcomes will
be utilized in the MANAGE function to assist risk monitoring and response efforts. It is incumbent on Framework users to continue applying the MEASURE function to AI systems
as knowledge, methodologies, risks, and impacts evolve over time.

likely to change over time as AI systems, policies, and norms evolve. Different organizations may have varied risk tolerances due to their particular organizational priorities and

Emerging knowledge and methods to better inform harm/cost-benefit tradeoffs will continue to be developed and debated by businesses, governments, academia, and civil society.
To the extent that challenges for specifying AI risk tolerances remain unresolved, there may
be contexts where a risk management framework is not yet readily applicable for mitigating
negative AI risks.
The Framework is intended to be flexible and to augment existing risk practices
which should align with applicable laws, regulations, and norms. Organizations
should follow existing regulations and guidelines for risk criteria, tolerance, and
response established by organizational, domain, discipline, sector, or professional
requirements. Some sectors or industries may have established definitions of harm or
established documentation, reporting, and disclosure requirements. Within sectors,
risk management may depend on existing guidelines for specific applications and

established documentation, reporting, and disclosure requirements. Within sectors,
risk management may depend on existing guidelines for specific applications and
use case settings. Where established guidelines do not exist, organizations should
define reasonable risk tolerance. Once tolerance is defined, this AI RMF can be used
to manage risks and to document risk management processes.
1.2.3
Risk Prioritization
Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because
not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may
lead organizations to allocate resources in a manner that makes risk triage inefficient or
impractical or wastes scarce resources. A risk management culture can help organizations
recognize that not all AI risks are the same, and resources can be allocated purposefully.
Actionable risk management efforts lay out clear guidelines for assessing trustworthiness
of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources should be
prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system. The extent
to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the
AI deployer can be a contributing factor.

applicable international standards, guidelines, and practices. As the AI RMF is put into

valid and reliable, safe, secure and resilient, accountable and transparent, explainable and
interpretable, privacy enhanced, and fair with their harmful biases managed.
Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,

(e.g., 1.1). All changes will be tracked using a Version Control Table which identifies the history, including
version number, date of change, and description of change. NIST plans to update the AI RMF Playbook

results.title: External reports
results.requirement: Describe how the Model Report provides or references any available external reports from independent external model evaluators (Appendix 3.5) and independent external security reviews (Appendix 4.5), subject to confidentiality and evaluator control of publication, and how the report addresses cases where no external evaluator was involved or where evaluator selection must be justified.
results.assessment_question: Does the Model Report (i) include or link to any available reports from independent external evaluators and independent external security reviews in a manner consistent with confidentiality and evaluator control, (ii) justify the absence of an external evaluator where applicable, and (iii) explain evaluator selection based on qualification criteria when an evaluator was involved?
expected_evidence: The Model Report includes or references (e.g., via valid hyperlinks) any available reports from independent external evaluators involved under Appendix 3.5, and any available independent external security review reports under Appendix 4.5, where sharing is compatible with confidentiality obligations and external-party control over publication.
The Model Report indicates that inclusion of external reports does not imply endorsement of their content by the Signatory.

If no independent external evaluator was involved, the Model Report provides a justification referencing the applicable exception conditions (e.g., similarly safe or safer model, or inability to appoint qualified evaluators despite early search efforts).

If at least one independent external evaluator was involved, the Model Report explains the choice of evaluator with reference to qualification criteria (e.g., domain expertise, technical evaluation experience, appropriate security protocols, confidentiality protections).
results.reasoning: None of the four indicators in the Expected Evidence are present: references to external evaluators (Appendix 3.5), external security reviews (Appendix 4.5), the statement that inclusion does not imply endorsement, and the justification/selection criteria for external evaluators. The absence cannot be offset by internal TEVV content, as SS-7.4 requires explicit external evaluator governance and publication controls.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: The Model Report does not address external evaluations or independent external security reviews as required by EU SS-7.4; it lacks references to Appendix 3.5/4.5, evaluator control statements, and justification or selection criteria for external evaluators.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The retrieved text does not address external evaluations or independent external security reviews, nor justify their absence or document evaluator selection, as required by the EU Code of Practice.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: No alignment to the external evaluator/reference requirements is evident; the text focuses on internal TEVV and measurement without referencing external reports or evaluator selection criteria.

alignment_overreach: No alignment to external evaluator/reference requirements is supported by the retrieved text; there is no evidence of external report references, confidentiality controls, or evaluator selection justification.

results.requirement: Describe, in the Model Report, information relevant for understanding whether and how the development, making available on the market, and/or use of the model results in material changes to the systemic risk landscape that are relevant for systemic risk assessment and mitigation under this Chapter.
results.assessment_question: Does the Model Report describe whether and how the model results in material changes to the systemic risk landscape, in a way that supports understanding of implications for systemic risk assessment and mitigation?
expected_evidence: The Model Report includes information enabling understanding of whether and how the model leads to material changes in the systemic risk landscape relevant for systemic risk assessment and mitigation.
The Model Report describes scaling effects or scaling laws that suggest novel or materially enhanced model capabilities, where applicable.
The Model Report summarises characteristics of novel model architectures that materially improve computational efficiency or capabilities, where applicable.
The Model Report describes information relevant to assessing changes in mitigation effectiveness (e.g., reduced human legibility of chain-of-thought or other safety-relevant properties).
The Model Report describes training techniques that materially improve the efficiency or feasibility of training (e.g., distributed or large-scale training), where applicable.

Approaches for measuring impacts on a population work best if they recognize that contexts

Risk at different stages of the AI lifecycle: Measuring risk at an earlier stage in the AI
lifecycle may yield different results than measuring risk at a later stage; some risks may
be latent at a given point in time and may increase as AI systems adapt and evolve. Furthermore, different AI actors across the AI lifecycle can have different risk perspectives.
For example, an AI developer who makes AI software available, such as pre-trained models, can have a different risk perspective than an AI actor who is responsible for deploying
that pre-trained model in a specific use case. Such deployers may not recognize that their
particular uses could entail risks which differ from those perceived by the initial developer.
All involved AI actors share responsibilities for designing, developing, and deploying a
trustworthy AI system that is fit for purpose.

roles and responsibilities, culture, and incentive structures for risk management to be effective. Use of the AI RMF alone will not lead to these changes or provide the appropriate

senior levels and may require cultural change within an organization or industry. In addition, small to medium-sized organizations managing AI risks or implementing the AI RMF
may face different challenges than large organizations, depending on their capabilities and
resources.

results.title: AI Office notification
results.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework acknowledges the obligation to provide the AI Office with access to the Model Report and any updates, including timing requirements, permitted delays, interim reporting, and conditions for redactions in line with Measure 7.7.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework acknowledge and describe obligations to provide the AI Office with access to the Model Report and updates, including timing rules, permitted delays with interim reporting, and conditions for redactions?
expected_evidence: The framework states that the AI Office must be provided with access to the Model Report by the time a model is placed on the market.
The framework specifies that updates to the Model Report must be made accessible to the AI Office within a defined timeframe (e.g. five business days).
The framework acknowledges conditions under which redactions may be applied, such as requirements arising from national security laws.
The framework describes the possibility of delaying provision of the Model Report or updates for a limited period (e.g. up to 15 business days), subject to good-faith conditions.
The framework requires or acknowledges the provision of an interim Model Report containing specified information when such a delay is used.
The framework describes acceptable access mechanisms (e.g. publicly accessible link or secure channel specified by the AI Office).
results.reasoning: None of the six indicators are present in the text: no obligation for AI Office access to the Model Report by market entry, no defined timeframe for updates, no redaction conditions, no allowed delays, no interim Model Report, and no specified access mechanism. The missing operational provisions cannot be offset by general governance language.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: An obligation for the AI Office to be provided access to the Model Report by the time a model is placed on the market.
A defined timeframe for making Model Report updates accessible to the AI Office (e.g., within five business days).
Conditions under which redactions may be applied (e.g., in accordance with national security or other legal requirements).
Allowance for delaying the provision of the Model Report or updates for a limited period (e.g., up to 15 business days) under good-faith conditions.
Provision of an interim Model Report containing specified information when such a delay is used.
Specified access mechanisms (e.g., a publicly accessible link or a secure channel designated by the AI Office).

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: No — the provided AI RMF text does not acknowledge or describe obligations to provide an AI Office with access to a Model Report or updates, nor timing rules, permitted delays with interim reporting, or redaction conditions.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The text covers general risk governance and openness but provides no operational provisions about Model Reports or external access by an AI Office, so it does not align with the specific SS-7.7 obligations. It remains conceptual rather than implementing the required operational mechanisms.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The external framework lacks any obligation or mechanism to provide the AI Office with access to the Model Report or its updates, including timing rules, permitted delays with interim reporting, redaction conditions, and defined access methods.
missing_elements: An obligation for the AI Office to be provided access to the Model Report by the time a model is placed on the market.
A defined timeframe for making Model Report updates accessible to the AI Office (e.g., within five business days).
Conditions under which redactions may be applied (e.g., in accordance with national security or other legal requirements).
Allowance for delaying the provision of the Model Report or updates for a limited period (e.g., up to 15 business days) under good-faith conditions.
Provision of an interim Model Report containing specified information when such a delay is used.
Specified access mechanisms (e.g., a publicly accessible link or a secure channel designated by the AI Office).
weaker_areas: General risk governance and openness are present, but there are no binding, operational obligations or processes for external regulatory access to the Model Report or updates.
scope_divergences: Divergence from the EU requirement: the EU measure specifies external oversight and formal access rights to the Model Report by an AI Office with defined timing and redaction provisions, whereas the external framework focuses on internal risk management without addressing external access obligations.

synthesis_result.justification: None of the six indicators are present in the text: no obligation for AI Office access to the Model Report by market entry, no defined timeframe for updates, no redaction conditions, no allowed delays, no interim Model Report, and no specified access mechanism. The missing operational provisions cannot be offset by general governance language.
