criteria.title: AI Office notification
criteria.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework acknowledges the obligation to provide the AI Office with access to the Model Report and any updates, including timing requirements, permitted delays, interim reporting, and conditions for redactions in line with Measure 7.7.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework acknowledge and describe obligations to provide the AI Office with access to the Model Report and updates, including timing rules, permitted delays with interim reporting, and conditions for redactions?
expected_evidence: The framework states that the AI Office must be provided with access to the Model Report by the time a model is placed on the market.
The framework specifies that updates to the Model Report must be made accessible to the AI Office within a defined timeframe (e.g. five business days).
The framework acknowledges conditions under which redactions may be applied, such as requirements arising from national security laws.
The framework describes the possibility of delaying provision of the Model Report or updates for a limited period (e.g. up to 15 business days), subject to good-faith conditions.
The framework requires or acknowledges the provision of an interim Model Report containing specified information when such a delay is used.
The framework describes acceptable access mechanisms (e.g. publicly accessible link or secure channel specified by the AI Office).
criteria.reasoning: None of the six indicators are present in the text: no obligation for AI Office access to the Model Report by market entry, no defined timeframe for updates, no redaction conditions, no allowed delays, no interim Model Report, and no specified access mechanism. The missing operational provisions cannot be offset by general governance language.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: An obligation for the AI Office to be provided access to the Model Report by the time a model is placed on the market.
A defined timeframe for making Model Report updates accessible to the AI Office (e.g., within five business days).
Conditions under which redactions may be applied (e.g., in accordance with national security or other legal requirements).
Allowance for delaying the provision of the Model Report or updates for a limited period (e.g., up to 15 business days) under good-faith conditions.
Provision of an interim Model Report containing specified information when such a delay is used.
Specified access mechanisms (e.g., a publicly accessible link or a secure channel designated by the AI Office).

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: No — the provided AI RMF text does not acknowledge or describe obligations to provide an AI Office with access to a Model Report or updates, nor timing rules, permitted delays with interim reporting, or redaction conditions.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The text covers general risk governance and openness but provides no operational provisions about Model Reports or external access by an AI Office, so it does not align with the specific SS-7.7 obligations. It remains conceptual rather than implementing the required operational mechanisms.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The external framework lacks any obligation or mechanism to provide the AI Office with access to the Model Report or its updates, including timing rules, permitted delays with interim reporting, redaction conditions, and defined access methods.
missing_elements: An obligation for the AI Office to be provided access to the Model Report by the time a model is placed on the market.
A defined timeframe for making Model Report updates accessible to the AI Office (e.g., within five business days).
Conditions under which redactions may be applied (e.g., in accordance with national security or other legal requirements).
Allowance for delaying the provision of the Model Report or updates for a limited period (e.g., up to 15 business days) under good-faith conditions.
Provision of an interim Model Report containing specified information when such a delay is used.
Specified access mechanisms (e.g., a publicly accessible link or a secure channel designated by the AI Office).
weaker_areas: General risk governance and openness are present, but there are no binding, operational obligations or processes for external regulatory access to the Model Report or updates.
scope_divergences: Divergence from the EU requirement: the EU measure specifies external oversight and formal access rights to the Model Report by an AI Office with defined timing and redaction provisions, whereas the external framework focuses on internal risk management without addressing external access obligations.

As directed by the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020 (P.L. 116-283),
the goal of the AI RMF is to offer a resource to the organizations designing, developing,
deploying, or using AI systems to help manage the many risks of AI and promote trustworthy and responsible development and use of AI systems. The Framework is intended to be
voluntary, rights-preserving, non-sector-specific, and use-case agnostic, providing flexibility to organizations of all sizes and in all sectors and throughout society to implement the
approaches in the Framework.
The Framework is designed to equip organizations and individuals – referred to here as
AI actors – with approaches that increase the trustworthiness of AI systems, and to help
foster the responsible design, development, deployment, and use of AI systems over time.
AI actors are defined by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
(OECD) as “those who play an active role in the AI system lifecycle, including organizations and individuals that deploy or operate AI” [OECD (2019) Artificial Intelligence in
Society—OECD iLibrary] (See Appendix A).
The AI RMF is intended to be practical, to adapt to the AI landscape as AI technologies
continue to develop, and to be operationalized by organizations in varying degrees and
capacities so society can benefit from AI while also being protected from its potential
harms.

criteria.title: Responsibilities
criteria.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines clear responsibilities for managing systemic risks, including systemic risk oversight, ownership, support and monitoring, and assurance, and how these responsibilities are allocated across organisational governance levels.
criteria.assessment_question: How must signatories assign systemic risk oversight, ownership, support and monitoring, and assurance responsibilities across the management body in its supervisory and executive functions, operational teams, and internal and external assurance providers, including role-specific requirements such as separation from core business activities and cascading responsibility structures for SMEs and SMCs?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly defines responsibilities for systemic risk oversight, ownership, support and monitoring, and assurance.
The framework describes how systemic risk oversight is assigned to a supervisory or otherwise independent governance function.
The framework describes how systemic risk ownership is assigned to executive-level functions responsible for risk-producing activities.
The framework describes how systemic risk support and monitoring is assigned to functions that are organisationally independent from core business activities.
The framework describes how systemic risk assurance is provided to a supervisory or independent body, including internal and, where applicable, external assurance.
The framework acknowledges proportional allocation of responsibilities based on organisational size and complexity (e.g. SMEs or SMCs).
criteria.reasoning: Found indicators: executive-level ownership of AI risk decisions; documented roles/responsibilities; SME/SMC proportional considerations; inventory and resource allocation for risk management. Missing: explicit systemic risk oversight as a separate supervisory/independent function; independence of risk support/monitoring; external assurance mechanisms; explicit cascading structures for SMEs/SMCs; explicit proportional allocation defined operationally. These missing indicators cannot be offset by thematic alignment.
key_aligned_concepts: Executive leadership ownership of AI risk decisions
Documented roles and lines of communication for AI risk
Cross-cutting governance integration across risk management
Ongoing monitoring and periodic review of risk management
SME/SMC proportional considerations in risk governance
Resource inventory/allocation for risk management
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: No explicit separate systemic risk oversight function (supervisory/independent)
No independent risk support/monitoring function clearly defined
No explicit external assurance mechanisms (internal and/or external) described
No explicit cascading risk responsibility structures for SMEs/SMCs
No explicit binding, operational proportional allocation by size/complexity

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: While the NIST AI RMF 1.0 text establishes governance structures, executive ownership, documented roles/responsibilities, and ongoing monitoring for AI risk, it does not explicitly define systemic risk oversight/ownership/assurance as distinct, independently supported functions or address SME/SMC cascading structures or external assurance as required by the EU Code of Practice.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: Partial alignment: it covers executive ownership, documented roles, and ongoing monitoring, which map to parts of the EU requirement, but it lacks explicit systemic risk oversight as a separate supervisory function, independence for risk support/monitoring, external assurance provisions, and SME/SMC cascading structures.

evidence_citations.quote: GOVERN 2.3: Executive leadership of the organization takes responsibility for decisions about risks associated with AI system development and deployment.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Supports EU requirement that ownership of risk decisions rests at executive level responsible for risk-producing activities.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Executive-level ownership of AI/systemic risk decisions.

evidence_citations.quote: GOVERN 2: Accountability structures are in place so that the appropriate teams and individuals are empowered, responsible, and trained for mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Demonstrates defined responsibilities across organization for AI risk management.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Explicitly defined responsibilities for risk oversight/ownership and monitoring.

evidence_citations.quote: GOVERN 2.1: Roles and responsibilities and lines of communication related to mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks are documented and are clear to individuals and teams throughout the organization.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Aligns with EU requirement for clear allocation of risk management roles across governance levels.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Documentation and clarity of roles/responsibilities for risk management.

evidence_citations.quote: GOVERN is a cross-cutting function that is infused throughout AI risk management and enables the other functions of the process.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Supports the concept of governance across organization.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Governance is integrated across all risk management functions.

evidence_citations.quote: GOVERN 1.5: Ongoing monitoring and periodic review of the risk management process and its outcomes are planned and organizational roles and responsibilities clearly defined, including determining the frequency of periodic review.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Directly covers ongoing oversight and defined responsibilities, a core EU Code requirement.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Ongoing monitoring and defined roles/responsibilities for monitoring.

evidence_citations.quote: In addition, small to medium-sized organizations managing AI risks or implementing the AI RMF may face different challenges than large organizations, depending on their capabilities and resources.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Addresses SME/SMC considerations within governance of AI risk.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Proportional allocation of responsibilities based on organisation size/complexity (SMEs/SMCs).

evidence_citations.quote: GOVERN 1.6: Mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems and are resourced according to organizational risk priorities.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Supports governance and allocation of risk management resources across the organization.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Resource allocation and inventory of AI systems for risk management.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The NIST AI RMF 1.0 governance text does not explicitly define a separate systemic risk oversight function or formal external assurance mechanisms, and it lacks explicit SME/SMC cascading structures and independence of risk support/monitoring from core business activities.
missing_elements: Explicit definition of systemic risk oversight as a distinct supervisory/independent function.
Formal framework for assurance to a supervisory or independent body, including internal and external assurance.
Explicit independence of risk support and monitoring functions from core business activities.
Explicit cascading risk responsibility structures for SMEs and SMCs (i.e., proportional, tiered allocation of duties across smaller entities).
Explicit proportional allocation of systemic risk responsibilities based on organisational size and complexity.
weaker_areas: Independence of risk support/monitoring from core business activities is not clearly established (text describes governance as cross-cutting rather than independent).
Proportional allocation by size/complexity is acknowledged but not defined in binding, operational terms.
External assurance provisions are not described (internal/external assurance mechanisms are not specified).
Explicit cascading responsibility structures for SMEs/SMCs are not described.
scope_divergences: EU requirement envisions a supervisory/independent governance function for systemic risk oversight, while the text presents governance as a cross-cutting, integrated function with executive ownership; no standalone supervisory/independent oversight layer is defined.
External assurance and SME/SMC cascading structures are not articulated, diverging from the EU's emphasis on independent assurance and proportional, cascadeable responsibility allocation.

synthesis_result.justification: Found indicators: executive-level ownership of AI risk decisions; documented roles/responsibilities; SME/SMC proportional considerations; inventory and resource allocation for risk management. Missing: explicit systemic risk oversight as a separate supervisory/independent function; independence of risk support/monitoring; external assurance mechanisms; explicit cascading structures for SMEs/SMCs; explicit proportional allocation defined operationally. These missing indicators cannot be offset by thematic alignment.

criteria.title: Risk culture
criteria.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework promotes a healthy systemic risk culture, including leadership tone, openness to challenge, independence of systemic risk functions, and protections for reporting and whistleblowing.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework explicitly acknowledge the importance of a healthy systemic risk culture and describe principles or mechanisms intended to promote it?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly recognises the importance of promoting a healthy systemic risk culture.
The framework describes leadership responsibilities or tone-from-the-top communication regarding systemic risk.
The framework states that challenge, escalation, or critical discussion of systemic risk decisions is encouraged.
The framework describes independence or safeguards for actors involved in systemic risk assessment and mitigation.
The framework references internal reporting or whistleblowing channels related to systemic risks.
The framework includes a non-retaliation commitment or protection for individuals raising systemic risk concerns.
criteria.reasoning: Evidence shows only one indicator met (recognition of a healthy risk culture). The indicators for leadership tone/from-the-top, escalation/challenge mechanisms, independence safeguards, internal reporting channels, whistleblower protections, and non-retaliation protections are not evidenced. Because these operational elements are missing and cannot be offset by thematic alignment alone, the criterion is not satisfied in full.
key_aligned_concepts: Enhanced organizational culture prioritizing AI risk management
Better information sharing about risks and TEVV practices
Strengthened engagement with interested parties and relevant AI actors
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Missing explicit leadership tone/from-the-top messaging on systemic risk
No formal encouragement of challenge, escalation, or critical discussion of systemic risk decisions
Lack of independence safeguards for actors involved in systemic risk assessment and mitigation
Absence of internal reporting channels specific to systemic risks
No whistleblower protections for individuals reporting systemic risk concerns
No non-retaliation commitment protecting individuals raising systemic risk concerns
Scope divergence: text focuses on AI risk management within AI RMF rather than enterprise-wide systemic risk governance

criteria.title: Incident identification
criteria.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines methods and channels for identifying and tracking serious incidents across the model lifecycle, including consideration of external sources and facilitation of third-party reporting.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework acknowledge and describe approaches for identifying serious incidents, including monitoring external sources and enabling third-party reporting?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly recognises the need to identify and track serious incidents across the model lifecycle.
The framework describes intended methods for identifying serious incidents, including reference to post-market monitoring or similar processes.
The framework references consideration of external information sources (e.g. media, incident databases, research, public reporting).
The framework describes how downstream providers, users, or other third parties may report serious incidents to the Signatory and/or authorities.
criteria.reasoning: All five expected indicators are unmet. The text does not provide explicit methods for identifying and tracking serious incidents across the lifecycle, external information sources, third-party reporting channels, or post-market monitoring. It only references lifecycle governance and generic monitoring of third-party resources, which is not sufficient to satisfy operational indicators; thus alignment alone cannot compensate.
key_aligned_concepts: Lifecycle governance across AI risk management (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE)
Monitoring of AI risks from third-party resources (MANAGE 3.1)
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit methods and channels for incident identification and reporting are missing; no post-market monitoring or external-source data flows; no third-party reporting mechanisms to authorities.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The retrieved text does not explicitly describe how to identify and track serious incidents across the model lifecycle via external sources or third‑party reporting channels; it mainly references lifecycle governance and monitoring of third‑party resources but lacks concrete incident- identification and reporting mechanisms.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: Limited alignment: it recognizes lifecycle governance (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) and mentions monitoring of third-party resources, but provides no explicit methods, channels, or processes for identifying and reporting serious incidents to authorities or signatories.
key_aligned_concepts: Lifecycle governance across AI risk management (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE)
Monitoring of AI risks from third-party resources (MANAGE 3.1)

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The text does not provide explicit methods, channels, or processes for identifying and tracking serious incidents across the AI lifecycle, including incorporation of external sources and third-party reporting to signatories or authorities.
missing_elements: Explicit methods and criteria for identifying serious incidents across the full AI lifecycle (from development through deployment and post-market) rather than general risk monitoring.
Defined channels and procedures for obtaining information from external sources (e.g., media, incident databases, research, public reporting) to identify potential serious incidents.
Mechanisms for third-party reporting to Signatories and/or authorities, including report submission pathways, data requirements, and escalation procedures.
A post-market monitoring or equivalent process specifically for identifying, tracking, and reporting serious incidents once AI systems are deployed.
Clear data retention, reporting timelines, and accountability for incident information across the lifecycle.
weaker_areas: MANAGE 3.1’s statement that AI risks and benefits from third-party resources are regularly monitored; it lacks concrete incident-identification criteria, data flows, and reporting obligations to authorities.
Reference to lifecycle governance (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) without explicit operational provisions for incident identification or reporting.
scope_divergences: EU requirement expects description of methods and channels for identifying and tracking serious incidents across the model lifecycle, including external sources and third-party reporting; the retrieved text does not address these aspects explicitly and focuses only on general governance and third-party monitoring.
alignment_overreach: Claims that the text covers 'identifying and tracking serious incidents across the model lifecycle' and 'external sources and third-party reporting channels' are not supported by the retrieved text.

synthesis_result.justification: All five expected indicators are unmet. The text does not provide explicit methods for identifying and tracking serious incidents across the lifecycle, external information sources, third-party reporting channels, or post-market monitoring. It only references lifecycle governance and generic monitoring of third-party resources, which is not sufficient to satisfy operational indicators; thus alignment alone cannot compensate.
key_aligned_concepts: Lifecycle governance across AI risk management (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE)
Monitoring of AI risks from third-party resources (MANAGE 3.1)
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit methods and channels for incident identification and reporting are missing; no post-market monitoring or external-source data flows; no third-party reporting mechanisms to authorities.

criteria.title: Incident documentation
criteria.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines the information that should be tracked, documented, and reported for serious incidents, including root cause analysis, mitigation failures or circumvention, and handling of incomplete information.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework specify the minimum information set for serious incident documentation and reporting, including root cause analysis and treatment of missing information?
expected_evidence: The framework defines the categories of information to be documented for serious incidents (e.g. timing, harm, affected groups, model involvement, and response actions).
The framework specifies that a root cause analysis should be conducted, including examination of model outputs, inputs, and any failures or circumvention of systemic risk mitigations.
The framework describes how patterns or signals from post-market monitoring may inform incident analysis.
The framework acknowledges that some information may be unavailable at the time of reporting and requires such gaps to be explicitly recorded.
The framework indicates that the level of detail in serious incident documentation should be proportionate to the severity of the incident.
criteria.reasoning: Found evidence of post-deployment monitoring and incident tracking/reporting to AI actors, but explicit minimum information categories, root-cause analysis requirements, handling of missing information, and severity-based detail guidance are not specified; thus core operational indicators are unmet and cannot be fully offset by thematic alignment.
key_aligned_concepts: Post-deployment monitoring plans
Incidents tracking, reporting, and communication to AI actors
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit minimum information set for serious incidents (timing, harm, affected groups, model involvement, response actions) is missing.
Mandated root cause analysis addressing model outputs, inputs, and failures or circumvention of systemic risk mitigations is absent.
Clear mechanism showing how patterns or signals from post-market monitoring inform incident analysis is absent.
Explicit handling of incomplete information, including recording information gaps in reports, is lacking.
Guidance that the level of detail in documentation should be proportionate to incident severity is not provided.
Defined reporting timelines, retention periods, and regulatory notification obligations for serious incidents are not specified.
Mitigation failures or circumvention as part of root cause assessment is not explicitly referenced.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The AI RMF 1.0 text does not explicitly specify the minimum information set for serious incident documentation and reporting (root cause analysis and handling of missing information) as required by SS-9.2, though it describes operational incident tracking, reporting, and post-deployment monitoring processes.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: Partial alignment at the operational level (incident tracking/reporting and post-deployment monitoring) but lacking explicit minimum information categories, root-cause analysis requirements, and handling of incomplete information as per the EU criterion.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: AI RMF 1.0 does not specify an explicit minimum information set for serious incident documentation and reporting, nor require explicit root cause analysis or handling of missing information. It also lacks clearly defined information categories (timing, harm, affected groups, model involvement, and response actions), explicit use of post-market signals for incident analysis, and guidance on reporting timelines or severity-based detail.

Explicit reference to mitigation failures or circumvention as part of root cause assessment.
Explicit criteria or thresholds for what constitutes a serious incident requiring formal documentation and escalation.

criteria.title: Reporting timelines
criteria.requirement: The framework defines mandatory severity-based reporting timelines for serious incidents involving the model, including differentiated deadlines for initial reports based on incident type, requirements for periodic intermediate updates for unresolved incidents, and submission of a final report after incident resolution.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework specify clearly differentiated reporting timelines for serious incidents (including specific deadlines for initial notification based on severity), periodic intermediate updates for unresolved incidents, and a final report after resolution?
expected_evidence: The framework defines categories of serious incidents (e.g., critical infrastructure disruption, cybersecurity breach, death, serious harm to health, fundamental rights, property or environment).
The framework associates specific deadlines for initial reporting following awareness of a serious incident (e.g., two days, five days, ten days, fifteen days depending on severity).
The framework clarifies that reporting is triggered when the organisation becomes aware of the involvement of its model, including cases of reasonable suspicion of causal linkage.
The framework specifies periodic intermediate updates for unresolved serious incidents (e.g., at least every four weeks after the initial report).
The framework defines a deadline for submitting a final report after resolution of the serious incident (e.g., within 60 days after resolution).
The framework allows aggregation of multiple similar serious incidents within defined reporting timelines while respecting the earliest applicable deadline.
criteria.reasoning: Only the awareness-based reporting trigger is evidenced (1 of 6 indicators). Missing are severity-based incident Categories, initial reporting deadlines tied to severity, explicit severity-based triggering, periodic updates, final resolution report deadline, and aggregation rules. These operational requirements cannot be offset by the single trigger concept.
key_aligned_concepts: Trigger-based reporting on awareness of model involvement
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Missing explicit severity-based categories of serious incidents (categories with severity levels).
No defined, severity-based deadlines for initial reporting after awareness.
No explicit triggering conditions tied to incident severity beyond awareness.
No mandatory periodic intermediate updates for unresolved incidents (e.g., every four weeks).
No deadline for final report after resolution (e.g., within 60 days).
No mechanism to aggregate multiple similar incidents within defined timelines while respecting earliest deadline.
Lack of explicit alignment with categorized severity framework to EU requirements.

Risk Prioritization
Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because
not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may
lead organizations to allocate resources in a manner that makes risk triage inefficient or
impractical or wastes scarce resources. A risk management culture can help organizations
recognize that not all AI risks are the same, and resources can be allocated purposefully.
Actionable risk management efforts lay out clear guidelines for assessing trustworthiness
of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources should be
prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system. The extent
to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the
AI deployer can be a contributing factor.

criteria.title: Retention
criteria.requirement: Define and maintain retention requirements ensuring that serious-incident documentation is preserved for at least five years from the later of the documentation date or the incident date.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework define retention requirements for serious-incident documentation that meet or exceed a five-year period?
expected_evidence: The framework states that documentation of information related to serious incidents must be retained.
The framework specifies a minimum retention period of at least five years.
The framework indicates that the retention period is counted from the later of the documentation date or the date of the serious incident.
criteria.reasoning: No indicators are met: the framework does not state (1) that serious-incident documentation must be retained, (2) a minimum five-year retention period, or (3) that the five-year period starts from the later of the documentation date or incident date. Without these operational requirements, alignment with the EU rule is not satisfied.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit retention requirement: serious-incident documentation must be retained for a minimum of five years.

Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

practices, methodologies, and tools for managing AI risks – as well as illustrate the
need for additional, improved resources.

abilities to operate under applicable domestic and international legal or regulatory
regimes.

may consider leveraging available standards and guidance that provide broad guidance to
organizations to reduce security and privacy risks, such as, but not limited to, the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, the NIST Privacy Framework, the NIST Risk Management Framework, and the Secure Software Development Framework. These frameworks have some
features in common with the AI RMF. Like most risk management approaches, they are
outcome-based rather than prescriptive and are often structured around a Core set of functions, categories, and subcategories. While there are significant differences between these
frameworks based on the domain addressed – and because AI risk management calls for
addressing many other types of risks – frameworks like those mentioned above may inform
security and privacy considerations in the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions of the
AI RMF.
At the same time, guidance available before publication of this AI RMF does not comprehensively address many AI system risks. For example, existing frameworks and guidance
are unable to:
• adequately manage the problem of harmful bias in AI systems;
• confront the challenging risks related to generative AI;
• comprehensively address security concerns related to evasion, model extraction, membership inference, availability, or other machine learning attacks;
• account for the complex attack surface of AI systems or other security abuses enabled
by AI systems; and
